result: Pharmacological CRF1 receptor antagonism with antalarmin completely abolished morphine-induced sociability deficits in male C57BL/6J mice. Antalarmin/morphine-treated male mice spent more time with the unfamiliar conspecific than with the object (p < 0.005), did not differ from saline-treated mice in sociability ratio (p = 0.661), and showed higher sociability ratio than vehicle/morphine-treated mice (p < 0.005).
evaluation: Claims C1, C38-C41 provide converging behavioral evidence from the three-chamber test showing that antalarmin pretreatment prevented morphine-induced sociability deficits in male mice. The data include appropriate statistical comparisons with significant p-values and are supported by Figure 1C-D. The experimental design includes proper controls (vehicle/saline group) and the results are internally consistent.

result: Antalarmin did not abolish morphine-induced sociability deficits in female C57BL/6J mice. Morphine-treated female mice spent similar time with the unfamiliar conspecific and object (p = 0.259) and showed lower sociability ratio than saline-treated mice (p < 0.05), independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment.
evaluation: Claims C2, C43-C44 demonstrate that antalarmin was ineffective in preventing morphine-induced sociability deficits in female mice, with appropriate statistical support (lack of pretreatment × treatment interaction). This sex-specific difference is a key finding supported by Figure 1F-G and statistical analyses reported in Supplementary file 1d.

result: Genetic CRF1 receptor-deficiency eliminated morphine-induced sociability deficits and PVN neuronal firing in male mice in a gene expression-dependent manner. Morphine-treated CRF1 KO mice showed unaltered sociability and no increase in PVN neuronal firing, while CRF1 HET mice showed intermediate effects between WT and KO mice.
evaluation: Claims C3, C58-C62 provide complementary genetic evidence supporting the pharmacological findings. The gene dosage-dependent effects in CRF1 HET mice strengthen the conclusion that CRF1 receptor function is necessary for morphine-induced sociability deficits and PVN activation. Data are supported by Figures 3C-E with appropriate statistical analyses showing genotype × treatment interactions.

result: Antalarmin eliminated morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in male C57BL/6J mice. Vehicle/morphine-treated male mice showed higher firing frequency than vehicle/saline-treated mice (p < 0.0005), while antalarmin/morphine-treated mice did not differ from saline-treated mice (p = 0.552) and showed lower firing frequency than vehicle/morphine-treated mice (p < 0.005).
evaluation: Claims C4, C50-C52 demonstrate that antalarmin prevents morphine-induced PVN neuronal activation in male mice. The electrophysiology data (n=110 cells) are well-powered and show clear pretreatment × treatment interaction effects. Results are supported by Figure 2B with appropriate statistical analyses.

result: Antalarmin did not eliminate morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in female C57BL/6J mice. Morphine similarly increased firing frequency in vehicle- or antalarmin-pretreated female mice compared to saline-treated mice (p < 0.0005), with no pretreatment × treatment interaction effect.
evaluation: Claims C5, C53, C56 show that antalarmin was ineffective in preventing morphine-induced PVN neuronal activation in female mice (n=93 cells). The lack of pretreatment × treatment interaction and the statistical comparisons across sex (C54-C56) provide strong evidence for sex-specific CRF1 receptor involvement. Data are supported by Figure 2D.

result: Genetic CRF1 receptor-deficiency reduced morphine-induced firing of PVN neurons in a CRF1 gene expression-dependent manner. Morphine increased firing frequency in CRF1 WT (p < 0.0005) and CRF1 HET (p < 0.005) but not in CRF1 KO mice (p = 0.987), with CRF1 HET mice showing intermediate firing frequency.
evaluation: Claim C6 and supporting claims C58-C62 demonstrate gene dosage-dependent effects on PVN neuronal firing. The graded response across genotypes (WT > HET > KO) provides strong evidence for CRF1 receptor involvement. Data from 17-31 cells/group are supported by Figure 3E with appropriate statistical analyses showing genotype × treatment interactions.

result: The electrophysiology results consistently mirrored the behavioral results, indicating a link between morphine-induced PVN activity and sociability deficits. Both pharmacological and genetic disruption of CRF1 receptor function produced parallel effects on sociability and PVN neuronal firing in male mice.
evaluation: Claims C7, C57, C63 draw appropriate inferences from the parallel behavioral and electrophysiological findings. The consistency between antalarmin and CRF1 KO results across both behavioral and neural measures strengthens the conclusion of a mechanistic link. However, this remains correlative rather than demonstrating direct causation, as PVN-specific manipulations were not performed.

result: In male mice, antalarmin abolished morphine-induced firing in PVN neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP. Vehicle/morphine-treated male mice showed higher firing frequency of OXY/AVP-expressing neurons than vehicle/saline-treated mice (p < 0.0005), while antalarmin/morphine-treated mice did not differ from saline-treated mice (p = 0.782) and showed lower firing frequency than vehicle/morphine-treated mice (p < 0.0005).
evaluation: Claims C8, C65-C67 identify the specific neuronal population affected by CRF1 receptor antagonism in male mice. The immunohistochemical identification of recorded neurons (40 OXY+/AVP+ cells from 110 total) combined with electrophysiology provides cell-type-specific mechanistic insight. Data are supported by Figure 4C with appropriate statistical analyses.

result: In male mice, antalarmin did not abolish morphine-induced firing in neurons expressing only AVP. Morphine increased firing frequency of AVP-only neurons independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment (p < 0.05).
evaluation: Claims C9 and C68 demonstrate cell-type specificity of CRF1 receptor effects in male mice. The differential effects on OXY/AVP co-expressing versus AVP-only neurons (49 cells) suggest that CRF1 receptors specifically modulate OXY-expressing neuronal populations. Data are supported by Figure 4D.

result: In female mice, antalarmin did not affect morphine-induced firing of neurons co-expressing OXY and AVP. Morphine increased firing frequency of OXY/AVP co-expressing neurons independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment (p < 0.005).
evaluation: Claims C10 and C70 show that antalarmin does not prevent morphine-induced activation of OXY/AVP co-expressing neurons in female mice (31 cells). This sex-specific difference in CRF1 receptor involvement is consistent with the behavioral and overall PVN firing results. Data are supported by Figure 4F.

result: In female mice, antalarmin did not affect morphine-induced firing of neurons expressing only OXY. Morphine increased firing frequency of OXY-only neurons independently of vehicle or antalarmin pretreatment (p < 0.005).
evaluation: Claims C11 and C71 demonstrate that CRF1 receptor antagonism does not affect morphine-induced activation of OXY-only neurons in female mice (38 cells). This contrasts with the male-specific effects on OXY-expressing populations and supports the sex-specific role of CRF1 receptors. Data are supported by Figure 4G.

result: There is a selective sex-specific role for the CRF1 receptor in opiate-induced PVN OXY activity. CRF modulates brain OXY responses to opiate substances in a sex-dependent manner, with CRF1 receptor antagonism affecting OXY neuron firing in male but not female mice.
evaluation: Claims C12 and C72 appropriately synthesize the cell-type-specific findings across sexes. The differential effects of antalarmin on OXY-expressing neurons between males and females (C8-C11) provide strong evidence for sex-specific CRF-OXY interactions. However, the mechanisms underlying this sex difference remain speculative and require further investigation.

result: The findings demonstrate a major, sex-linked role for the CRF1 receptor in sociability deficits and related brain alterations induced by morphine. Both pharmacological and genetic disruption of CRF1 receptor function eliminated morphine-induced sociability deficits and PVN neuronal firing in male, but not female, mice.
evaluation: Claims C13 and C48 represent the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing behavioral and neural findings across pharmacological and genetic approaches. The convergence of evidence from antalarmin treatment and CRF1 KO mice, combined with parallel behavioral and electrophysiological effects specifically in males, strongly supports this conclusion. The sex-specific nature is well-documented across multiple measures.

result: The findings suggest a new therapeutic strategy for opiate use disorders through inhibition of CRF1 receptor activity, which may relieve severe social behavior deficits commonly observed in OUD patients.
evaluation: Claims C14 and C128 extrapolate from acute morphine effects in mice to potential clinical applications in OUD patients. While the preclinical findings are robust, several gaps exist: (1) the study examined acute morphine effects rather than chronic use or withdrawal, (2) only male mice showed CRF1-dependent effects, limiting generalizability, (3) translation from mouse sociability tests to human social dysfunction is uncertain, and (4) no data on whether CRF1 antagonism affects other aspects of OUD. The therapeutic potential requires validation in models more relevant to human OUD.

result: Male mice treated with antalarmin/morphine showed higher sociability ratio than female mice treated with antalarmin/morphine (p < 0.05), and male mice treated with vehicle/morphine showed higher PVN firing frequency than all other male and female groups (p < 0.0005).
evaluation: Claims C45, C54-C56 provide direct statistical comparisons across sex, supporting the sex-specific effects of CRF1 receptor manipulation. The three-way ANOVA analyses appropriately test for sex × pretreatment × treatment interactions. However, the almost-significant interaction for sociability ratio (p = 0.075) suggests the sex difference may be less robust than implied.

result: Morphine effects upon sociability were unrelated to locomotor activity. Morphine-treated male, but not female, mice traveled more distance than saline-treated mice (p < 0.05), independently of antalarmin pretreatment, while overall mice traveled more distance during habituation than sociability phase (p < 0.05).
evaluation: Claims C46-C47, C49, C90 demonstrate dissociation between locomotor and sociability effects. The observation that antalarmin and vehicle-treated male mice showed similar locomotor responses but different sociability responses to morphine (C49) supports this dissociation. However, the increased locomotor activity in morphine-treated males could still indirectly affect sociability measures, and the inference of complete independence may be overstated.

result: During the habituation phase, male C57BL/6J mice spent similar time in both ROIs, while morphine-treated female mice spent less time in the ROIs than saline-treated mice (p < 0.0005), independently of antalarmin pretreatment. Vehicle/morphine-treated male mice spent similar time with the unfamiliar conspecific and object (p = 0.823), indicating sociability deficits.
evaluation: Claims C36-C37, C42 describe baseline and morphine effects in the three-chamber test. The data demonstrate that morphine impairs sociability in both sexes but affects habituation behavior only in females. These findings are supported by appropriate statistical analyses and Figure 1B, E-F. The sex difference in habituation effects is interesting but its relationship to sociability deficits is unclear.

result: Immunohistochemical characterization revealed sex differences in PVN neuropeptide expression patterns. In male mice, a relatively large portion of cells expressed AVP but not OXY (49/110 cells), while in female mice, a large portion expressed OXY but not AVP (38/93 cells). These patterns are consistent with prior literature showing AVP- or OXY-positive neurons are more numerous in male or female PVN, respectively.
evaluation: Claims C64, C69, C103-C105 provide important characterization of the neuronal populations studied. The sex differences in neuropeptide expression patterns are well-documented and consistent with prior literature (C105). This characterization is essential for interpreting the cell-type-specific electrophysiology results. Data are supported by Figure 4B, E and immunohistochemistry methods.

result: Morphine (2.5 mg/kg) consistently and similarly decreased sociability in male and female mice, suggesting that unlike other behavioral effects of opiate substances, sex might have a marginal role in opiate-induced impairment of sociability.
evaluation: Claims C73 and C76 note that morphine impaired sociability similarly in both sexes, contrasting with sex differences in other opiate effects (C74-C75). This observation is supported by the current data and prior work (Piccin et al., 2022b). However, the inference that sex has a 'marginal role' in opiate-induced sociability impairment may be premature given that the mechanisms underlying these deficits are clearly sex-dependent (via CRF1 receptors in males but not females).

result: Male mice bearing a mixed (B6x129PF2/J) genetic background showed higher sociability levels than C57BL/6J male mice, and it is possible that the mixed (C57BL/6Jx129S4/SvJae) genetic background of the CRF1 receptor-deficient mice contributed to increased social approach compared to inbred C57BL/6J mice.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 acknowledge a potential confound in comparing CRF1 KO mice (mixed background) to C57BL/6J mice (inbred). The authors appropriately cite prior work (Moy et al., 2004) showing strain differences in sociability. However, despite this potential confound, the key finding that CRF1 KO mice do not show morphine-induced sociability deficits remains valid, as the comparison is between morphine and saline within the same genotype.

result: The similar results obtained with antalarmin and CRF1 KO mice argue in favor of a marginal role for the HPA axis in CRF1 receptor-mediated sociability deficits induced by morphine. Antalarmin does not affect basal or stress-induced ACTH and corticosterone levels, while CRF1 KO mice show HPA axis deficits.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 address a potential confound regarding HPA axis involvement. The argument that antalarmin (which doesn't affect HPA axis) produces similar effects to CRF1 KO (which has HPA deficits) suggests HPA-independent mechanisms. This logic is sound and supported by appropriate citations (C86-C88). However, the conclusion of a 'marginal role' for HPA axis may be overstated, as neither study directly measured HPA axis activity under the current experimental conditions.

result: Morphine consistently elevated the firing frequency of PVN neurons in male and female C57BL/6J mice and in male CRF1 WT and CRF1 HET mice. This likely reflects increased activity of PVN CRF neurons, as acute morphine treatment increases CRF levels in the hypothalamus and HPA axis activity, potentially through stimulation of presynaptic mu-opioid receptors on PVN GABA terminals.
evaluation: Claims C93-C96 describe the consistent effect of morphine on PVN neuronal firing and provide a mechanistic interpretation based on prior literature (C94-C95). The inference that morphine increases PVN CRF neuron activity (C96) is reasonable given the cited literature, though CRF expression was not directly measured in this study. The proposed mechanism involving mu-opioid receptors on GABA terminals is plausible but remains speculative without direct evidence.

result: Sex-linked differences in PVN CRF1 receptor expression, intracellular signaling, or cellular compartmentalization may contribute to the sex-linked behavioral and brain effects of antalarmin. Prior studies show sex differences in CRF and CRF1 receptor expression, CRF1 receptor-Gs coupling, and CRF1 receptor internalization.
evaluation: Claims C97-C102 propose potential mechanisms for the observed sex differences based on prior literature. While the cited studies (C97-C101) document sex differences in CRF system components, these were conducted in different brain regions (cortex, locus coeruleus) or under different conditions. The speculation that similar mechanisms operate in the PVN (C102) is reasonable but remains unvalidated. Direct measurement of PVN CRF1 receptor expression and signaling in the current experimental context would be needed to support this hypothesis.

result: Morphine disrupted sociability but increased firing of PVN neurons expressing OXY and/or AVP. PVN OXY neurons project to multiple brain areas where they may differentially modulate social behavior in a site-specific manner. Activation of PVN CRF1 receptors by morphine-induced CRF release might modulate the activity of PVN OXY neurons projecting to the VTA or BNST.
evaluation: Claims C106-C111, C114 attempt to reconcile the paradoxical finding that morphine increases OXY neuron firing while impairing sociability. The proposed explanation based on projection-specific effects (C107-C111) is supported by cited literature showing opposite effects of OXY in VTA versus BNST. However, the speculation about CRF1 receptor modulation of specific OXY projections (C114) lacks direct evidence. Projection-specific manipulations or recordings would be needed to test this hypothesis.

result: The morphine-induced firing of PVN OXY-positive neurons suggests a stress-like state that may disrupt social behavior. Morphine may activate brain CRF systems which, via CRF1 receptors, increase PVN OXY neuron activity to counteract stress effects. Pharmacological disruption of CRF1 receptors confers stress resilience that does not require PVN OXY activity.
evaluation: Claims C118-C124 propose an interpretive framework linking morphine effects to stress responses. While the cited literature (C118-C121) supports connections between stress, OXY, and CRF systems, the interpretation that morphine creates a 'stress-like state' requiring OXY activation for coping (C122-C123) is highly speculative. The alternative interpretation that CRF1 antagonism confers 'stress resilience' (C124) is also speculative and not directly tested. These hypotheses require validation through stress-related behavioral measures and direct assessment of stress markers.

result: There might be differential implication of the CRF1 receptor in social behavior deficits induced by acute opiate administration versus withdrawal from repeated administration. A single morphine administration may induce long-lasting behavioral and brain alterations relevant to substance use disorders, making it critical to identify neural substrates underlying initial opiate effects.
evaluation: Claims C79-C81 acknowledge limitations in comparing acute versus chronic/withdrawal paradigms and attempt to justify the relevance of acute studies. While C80 cites evidence that single morphine doses can have lasting effects, the differential involvement of CRF1 receptors in acute versus withdrawal states (C79) remains speculative. The claim that identifying substrates of initial opiate effects is 'critical' for treatment development (C81) may overstate the translational relevance of acute studies to chronic OUD.

result: The present results point to sex as a critical biological variable in studies assessing novel treatments for substance use disorders.
evaluation: Claim C129 appropriately emphasizes the importance of considering sex as a biological variable based on the robust sex differences observed throughout the study. The finding that CRF1 receptor antagonism is effective only in males has clear implications for treatment development and highlights the necessity of including both sexes in preclinical research. This conclusion is well-supported by the data.

result: Methodological details regarding animal sources, behavioral testing procedures, and drug dosing rationale. C57BL/6J mice were bred in-house from Janvier Labs stock. CRF1 receptor-deficient mice were bred from heterozygote matings and genotyped by PCR. The three-chamber test measured time in ROIs as a validated measure of sociability. Drug doses were chosen based on prior studies showing behavioral effects.
evaluation: Claims C130-C138 provide essential methodological information. The animal sources are clearly documented (C130-C131), the three-chamber test is appropriately described with validation from prior work (C132-C135), and drug doses are justified by citations to prior studies (C137-C138). These methodological details are adequately supported and allow for reproducibility. The validation of the sociability measure through correlation with nose-to-nose contacts (C134-C135) strengthens confidence in the behavioral assay.
